o ij Johannes Trithemius, abbot [unclear], sends greetings to the reader.

Since all the letters of the Greeks and the Hebrews are numerical, I have often wondered that the painstaking Latinity of the ancients did not also make its own letters serve the reckoning of numbers. The Hebrews, by a duplication of certain letters, established twenty-eight signs sufficient for every number. The Greeks, however, remedied this lack of letters with like foresight by adding four characters. Therefore, since we have twenty-four letters, why should we not also make ours numerical, since we can similarly find four to be duplicated? Let us give four as an example, and it will be quite enough for every number: m and final nj; likewise long s and final or closed s; likewise closed v and open u. When we add these to the twenty-four usual letters, we have twenty-eight characters sufficient for all numbers. Nor will it be a matter of great labor to grasp this method of numbering for those who already know letters, if once they commit it to memory.

For this invention of ours may be useful to many, since with few letters it comprises many thousands in number, all of which can be distinguished and understood at first sight, without any calculation, more clearly than by the figures of algorism, especially in large numbers, as seems to many who are less experienced in the art of calculation not to be possible so easily. For as soon as you have looked with your eye upon a number, however large, you will be able both fully to understand it and to express it without circumlocution or division of speech. Since this is easy, it is fitting that we set down the letters themselves reduced to number. I wrote this on 16 March, in the year 1509.

We have hitherto set forth, for example's sake, the manner of writing numbers by Latin letters [used by] the ancient Franks of Germany, that we might offer the knowledge of it also to those who do not know [it]. But that, in the placing of the figures of the algorism, we have departed from the common rule of computation, was done not from error but from a reasonable cause—namely, lest we be burdened in too great a progression. There were also [those] who wrote larger numbers in such a manner. [a third numeral table; partly garbled.]

These [matters] concerning the reckoning of numbers being duly completed, we end also the fifth book of Polygraphy. In the year of the Lord 1508.

[page 479:] The Sixth Book of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of Saint James the Greater the Apostle, of Würzburg, takes its beginning. Before every invention and use of letters, in the beginning of the world, when men were still rude in talent [and] uncultivated in morals—under the rule of the alternating communication of the three [intelligences], as some suppose, the intelligences succeeding one another in order through one thousand and sixty-three years—the influences of the planets were present in the world, in their own manner excelling [over] bodies on earth. The ancient speculators of this matter say that Saturn, from the beginning of the world, presided over the [things] germinating [and] being born on earth, by influence, his intelligence principally moderating [it]—which intelligence they named Orifiel, that is, the life-giving [intelligence] of God—for three hundred and fifty-four lunar years, four months, and as many days and hours. These [things] we recount as poetical, [and] do not confirm. After Saturn, Venus; after Venus, Jupiter is set down to have assumed the dominion. But after Jupiter, Mercury, fourth in order, as ruler, adorned the talents of men with diverse arts. But under the three intelligences mentioned—Saturn, namely, Venus, and Jupiter—ruling, they assert that men had not even the knowledge of letters. Whence, as often as one wished to announce something secret to another, he did this not by writings—since the office of letters was lacking—but by certain similitudes of animals, trees, plants, or of other sensible [things], symbolically, according as each had agreed among themselves. The time of Saturn gave to men, as they say, morals properly agreeing with [his] influence. For it made [them] farmers, hunters, founders of cities, rude, wild, sad, simple, uncultivated in life [and] morals, living long in the flesh. After Orifiel of Saturn, as those so opining [say], they say the intelligence Anael, the mover of Venus, [received] the governance of the world by influence, taking three hundred and fifty-four years…

[unclear], months, days, and four hours; under him men began to be more cultivated, to build houses more frequently, and cities, and also to invent various manual arts, namely the work of weaving, wool-working, and many other things similar to these. They also began to sink more deeply into the pleasures of the flesh, and, taking beautiful wives, with many children begotten from them, they fell notably away from natural simplicity. They invented games and songs; they began to play the cithara; whatever they maintained pertained to the influence of Venus, they devised with greater zeal, following too much the motion of the flesh.

They called the third intelligence of Jupiter Zachariel; receiving the dominion of the world after Anael, it made men restless with desire for rule, to go hunting, to make tents, to adorn themselves with various garments. While he held dominion, in accordance with the quality of Jupiter, who deprived his father of the kingdom, there arose a great division between the good and the wicked: the former invoking God, the latter given over to the flesh and the world. Under that rule Adam, the first man, died, leaving to all posterity the testament of dying once.

But the fourth mover, or angel, of Mercury, Raphael, influencing worldly things after Zachariel, began in the one thousand fifty-fifth year of the world, at the end of the month of February, and lasted until the one thousand four hundred tenth year of the world; under him the use of letters is said first to have been invented. The letters then, however, as they report, were different from those which the world has today, devised in the form and likeness of trees, plants, and animals; yet with time these were afterward altered in many ways, and took on an easier and more cultivated manner of being formed. For the fictions of the poets said that Mercury was the patron of all literature, promising that great hidden mysteries of things lay beneath their fables.

After this, when the human race had multiplied and had been spread everywhere over the whole earth, the unity of letters did not long remain; but the separation of bodies and minds far from one another discovered different and various modes of writing, concerning which a long narration would be needed from us. Plato the philosopher, in the Phaedrus, relates that a certain philosopher named Theotones first invented letters and the use of writing, together with the system of weights, numbers, and the game of dice, and taught Thamus, king of the Egyptians.

Concerning the rest, however, and the ancient men who are said to have handed down special letters to almost individual nations and peoples, which remain in use among them down to the present day, it is not my purpose on this occasion to set out or describe a narrative. For all our learned men know that Cadmus, son of Agenor, king of the Phoenicians, is said first to have brought sixteen letters into Greece: αβγδεζθκλμνοπρστυφψχω. [unclear] ε, κ, ω, λ, μ, β, ζ, σ, τ, ψ. To these Palamedes, at the time of the Trojan War, is reported to have added four: [unclear], θ, φ, χ. And afterward Pythagoras added the letter v, so that there should be twenty-one; and κ and ϖ were subsequently invented by others. Gordanis, bishop of the Goths, gave his people letters proper to them. When the unity of language had been confounded, the simplicity of characters was also varied in many ways. From this it happened that the use of letters, in the course of time, claimed such license for itself that not only individual peoples, but also individual men, fashioning new characters for letters at their own judgment, prepared hiding places for their mysteries.

Yet every writing in unusual characters will not be free from suspicion on the part of those who see it. Notwithstanding this, many kings, tyrants, and princes of old devised for themselves a private mode of writing, separated from the common one, caring little for the suspicion of others, provided that what they wished to remain secret was not perceived. Moved by imitation of them, and wishing to bring to a perfect end this work of the Polygraphia, so far as can be done, in this sixth book, which is also the last, I have determined to call back from the dead certain characters of the ancients which have long since ceased from mortal use, lest they perish utterly. And first indeed we shall set down the ancient manner of writing of the Northmen.

Concerning the Alphabet and the Manner of Writing

Of the Northmen, wonderful at that time when they were laying waste Gaul by their incursion.

All the letters of the Greeks and Palestinians are numerical, as was said before; while of the Latin letters, which we Germans also use, only seven [unclear] into numbers.

are referred to, namely c, d, i, l, m, v, and so forth. The Northmen, however, together with the Asiatic Dacians, having once come forth from the Scandinavian islands, which are now called Gothic, roamed through Gaul for more than forty years and devastated it most severely. In order to provide for their secret affairs, as Bede, the English monk, testifies, they devised from the letters of the Greeks the following new and handsome manner of writing. For they adapted the numerals of the Greeks, comprised in ten letters up to twenty-four, to Latin characters, and under a foreign form prudently concealed our letters, namely in the way in which we use numbers in place of letters: that is, for a we put 1, for b, 2, for c, 3, for d, 4, and so in sequence to the end of the alphabet. A handsome invention indeed, and sufficiently secure, which neither a Greek nor a Latin will easily understand. For the whole alphabet is not found in it, but only nine letters, and one numerical sign, namely g, which among them signifies six, and in this manner of writing f, the sixth letter of the Latins. Moreover, deferring to our German language, in which we were born, we have placed at the end the double w as the twenty-fourth letter of our nation, which, according to the Greek numeral, we formed thus: ꝟ. This writing of the Northmen, then, let us set down from the following order of Greek letters, in imitation of them.

This manner of writing can also be varied in many ways, when the letters are changed by transposition of the number. This can be done in the full Greek letters according to the wish and judgment of any industrious writer. Nor will the method of forming these characters be very difficult, especially for one who has had a little practice. The characters written above are also sufficiently suited to the German language, since with them we can denote all things that occur to us, in whatever speech we are skilled. Whenever iota is placed by itself, so that it may be known to denote the letter k, the tenth of the alphabet, it is marked above thus: ī.

Concerning the Alphabet and Method of Writing of the Ancient Franks.

[unclear]

The opinion of very many holds that the Germans once had letters from the Greeks, and they affirm firmly that they used the Greek language, especially in their sacred rites. For they say that there is a great consonance between the Greek language and our own, although the long interval of time has utterly extinguished that agreement. That most learned man, once my teacher, Johannes Camerarius Dalburgius, most reverend bishop of the church of Worms, had collected some thousands of Greek words which have the same meaning in both languages, Greek and German. And Caesar testifies in his Commentaries that the ancient Druids, the priests of sacred rites in Gaul, used the Greek language, especially in sacred matters. But when the Romans were devastating the world, they at length violently imposed the use of their own letters, together with their dominion, upon many nations. Finally the remnants of the Trojans, who afterward were called Franks, in the four-hundred[unclear] year before the incarnation of the Lord in the [unclear]-fortieth, having gone out from the borders of the Scythians, with King Marcomer furnishing leadership, they came into Germany, and received settlements from their Saxon brothers at the mouths of the Rhine. Thereafter, for nine hundred and fifty years, waging almost continual war with the Romans and Gauls, as Hunibald is the authority, they finally subjected almost all Europe to their command or kingdom. Yet, once they had received the letters of the Romans, they did not destroy them, but rather, being themselves mingled among the Germans and Gauls, they learned their language, and preserved their letters and the form of their writings. Vuasthaldus, a writer of the histories of this people, wrote books in his native speech on the deeds of kings, dukes, and princes over nearly seven hundred and fifty-eight years, with the characters appended, as Hunibald says, which he mentions in his volume that he published in eighteen books on the origin of the Franks.

Unless the fault of the scribe has deceived me, I have, as I think, suitably reproduced the alphabet of Wasthaldus; in it some characters differ entirely from the Greek, while some also seem partly to resemble them. Yet I do not know what I should judge: whoever their inventor may have been, although he did not preserve the form of the Greek letters, he nevertheless observed the order of the letters. The codex, falling apart from excessive age, could scarcely be read; hence I fear that I have rather been deceived by some interpolator than found the true and certain opinion of Hunibald.

But let us pass on to the things that remain, since if Hunibald's statement is true, it will have been well written by us; but if it is someone's fiction, it will neither harm us nor do injury to the reader. Another fictitious alphabet follows, found in the codex of Hunibald, to which this was inscribed:

The alphabet of the Franks, which Doracus invented.

Whoever wishes to use the characters written above should know that they are to be written beneath the lines, in the manner of the Greeks, not above as the Latins do. Likewise it must be observed that, of the double letters, the first are written at the beginning and in the middle of words, but the second always at the end.

From the grammarians of Otfridus, monk of Wissembourg.

We have read that Charles, king of the Franks, surnamed the Great, taking pity on the barbarism of his nation, with Nanno, Theobald, Albinus, and Berenger as helpers, attempted to bring the German language under rule. And although, as Turpin bears witness, he had begun so arduous a work, he did not complete it, being delayed by frequent incursions of wars, but, overtaken by death, left it unfinished; nor did another arise after him who would recall concern for this matter to his mind. But Otfridus, the aforesaid monk, formerly hearer and disciple of Rabanus Fuldaensis, under Louis the Pious, son of that Charles, having mastered that grammar, albeit imperfectly, wrote many things in our German language, which seem to sound with a remarkable weight of regular instruction, in meter both grave and elegiac; moreover he also composed some things in prose to Louis, king of Germany, son of Louis the Pious and brother of the emperor Lothar; also to Orgarius, archbishop of Mainz, to the monks of Saint Gall, and to others. Having obtained fragments of this grammar, I too have extracted the present characters of the alphabet from many, lest they utterly perish. Moreover it is established, on Otfridus' testimony, that Charles devised several alphabets of his own, by which he could safely use his very broad kingdom in secret matters with the individual prefects. From these, with Otfridus supplying them, we commit a few things to these letters.

Charles, the great king and most Christian emperor, fought with the Saxons for not less than thirty years; finally overcoming them by the sword, he converted them to the Christian faith. But fearing lest they should again apostatize from the faith, as they had done many times, he appointed certain secret investigators, to whom he granted judicial power, who, traveling through all Saxony, should secretly and diligently inquire concerning the faith and morals of the people; and whoever they found to have apostatized from the faith, robbers, adulterers, blasphemers, despisers of the church or of its priests and commands, or [those guilty] of notorious crimes against the Christian disturbing the public [peace?], or recalling or soliciting the people to paganism, they were, without delay, by imperial and royal authority and with impunity, to hang with a noose or otherwise kill as they could. But so that this institution might remain forever unshaken, he gave the same men power to substitute also others, fit under certain conditions, who, enjoying the aforesaid faculty, might with impunity exercise the office of inquisition and death against the guilty. Finally he prescribed for them secret laws, hidden signs, and also the form of an oath, by which they might proceed justly in judging and punishing, and, known to one another, might remain hidden from others, and might forever preserve the necessary, more secret tribunal in Saxon land. They also used certain alphabets among themselves for a time, which nevertheless in the end fell wholly out of use. Yet the office of an inquisition of this kind remains down to the present time, whose ministers are commonly called Feimers.

pleasing. For no one, however learned or trained in any language, becomes even a good writer unless by long practice of writing he has changed usage into art. Another also follows.

The first is that he form characters easy to draw; and the simpler they are, the better they will be. The second is that he arrange the individual letters so that, joined into words, they present a beautiful and elegant appearance. Vanity, fraud, deceitfulness, deception, sophification, greed, falsity, lying confidence, stupidity, want, poverty, despair, flight, proscription, and beggary are the attendants of alchemy, who, pretending to be the beloved mistress, keep her inviolate, and gladly offer themselves in her place to her moneyed, avaricious, greedy, and foolish seekers.

On the signs and wonderful but excessively laborious method of writing of M. T. Cicero, and afterward of Saint Cyprian, bishop and martyr.

Marcus Tullius Cicero, the eloquent orator of the Romans, wrote a book of signs of no small size, which Saint Cyprian, prelate of the Carthaginians, martyr, enlarged with many signs and words, adding vocabulary necessary for Christian uses, so that the work itself became not only more [unclear], but also [unclear] for the faithful.

The codex is rare, found by me only once, and bought at a cheap price. For in the year of the Lord’s Nativity 1496, when for love of books I was inspecting several libraries, I found the aforesaid codex in a certain monastery of our order, neglected through excessive age, cast away under dust and despised. I asked the abbot, a doctor of law, at what value he held it. He replied that he would prefer to it the little works of Saint Anselm, recently printed. I went to the booksellers, since the matter happened in a metropolitan city; I bought the requested little works of Anselm for a sixth part of a florin, gave them to the abbot and the rejoicing monks, and rescued the codex, already brought nearly to destruction. For, out of love of parchment, they had resolved that it should immediately be scraped.

Almost two years after this, when I went up to Strasbourg on business of my order, and was admitted by Johann Geiler of Kaysersberg, the distinguished preacher of the place, into the library of the greater church, I found a whole psalter written out in these same signs of Tullius and Cyprian, most fittingly written in gold at the head. But the title had been placed outside thus by someone ignorant of the mystery: “Psalter in the Armenian language.” I brought in a learned man, showed the falsity, and advised that it be retitled: “Psalter written in Ciceronian signs.” Whether he did so or not I am uncertain, since afterward I did not return to that library. That you may see, reader, the form of Cicero’s notation, we have determined to append a few signs.

[Table of signs and equivalents, partly unclear:] Vii = approves; W = modest; L = letter. 2i = approves; h = immodest; b = letter. 10 = wicked; M = moderate; g = syllable. 3 = upright; In = immoderate; k = time. A = uprightness; M = accommodating; t = [unclear]. B = wickedness; m = inconvenient; s = [unclear]. C = probable; T = accommodates; u = temporal. D = disapproves; S = beyond measure; v = extra-temporal. M = measure; H = in what way; y = man.

You need, indeed, a great memory for the method of writing, and an entirely immense labor of reading, where any character either signifies an entire word, or a final syllable, or some part of speech suitable for the composition of the whole. Therefore, all the signs being omitted, let us draw out an alphabet from a few.

[Alphabet of signs: unclear characters preserved in the Latin source.]

Many other new alphabets could also be formed from Cicero’s signs; we leave the drawing-out of them to the judgment of anyone who wishes to do it. For the book is very full, and contains many signs, notably differing from one another, all of which serve writers.

[Greek-letter alphabet.]

This was the alphabet of Iaimiclis, the great king of the [Articori?], surnamed Megalopius, a very wise man, which he used in secret matters; it too can be changed in many ways. To this, out of love for our prince, we have appended the following, in which, if it is more often used over time, writing will become easier.

[Greek-letter alphabet.]

How also by numbers and in many other various ways we can safely write any secrets whatever.

These things are childish, I admit, since everyone according to his own capacity and judgment can devise more numerous and more elegant alphabets than we have recorded in this volume. Therefore we knowingly omit many things which in a similar way are childish, common, and [unclear].

We judge it to be of little usefulness. We fear that someday we shall be ashamed to have turned our mind to these trifles, more useful matters having been set aside. But I pray that readers will spare me, since my own will did indeed draw me back from these childish studies, not to say at least partly vain ones; but the insistence of certain friends compelled me to write them, and indeed I could not refuse them this without injury to the bond of obligation contracted. Nevertheless, induced by their entreaty, I also had to connect the following chapter with the preceding matters, and to assign numbers for letters. For the ancients arranged various and manifold methods of writing under the figures of numbers, by which, through subtle invention, they safely transmitted their secrets to one another. Therefore, persuaded by the prayers of friends, we have placed a few methods out of many at the end of this sixth book, by which a path to knowledge of the others may lie open to those who do not know them. For if anyone delights to know these things, once these are known he will easily be able to ascend to higher matters, and to vary the methods discovered with manifold interchange at his own discretion. As the beginning of this matter, we have placed a table under the orchema, which, when the reading is varied in the manner of a cross, will contain ninety-six alphabets in itself.

In this figure we have placed, for each of the remaining six signs, individual alphabets by numbers, just as they are seen set beneath the Latin letters in order, so that anyone who wishes may more safely conceal his secrets by means of them.

We have, by God’s mercy, brought the sixth and last book of our Polygraphy to its close; in it, ending our discourse with the wandering stars, we give the reader advance warning on certain points.

First, whenever he uses the alphabet of any given [sign?], he should prudently attach it, for the sake of a double advantage. For by this excessive labor is removed from the friendly reader, and the secret will remain hidden, since anyone ignorant of the craft will suppose that a table written with numbers and marked beforehand with the characters of signs or planets pertains to the reckoning of astronomy, and will not at all suspect that any secret lies hidden. For that reason we have not taken up the official matter of the letters from unity, but from a distance, lest we give anyone any mark of suspicion. Nevertheless prudence must be used by writers, since a clever reader who is touched by suspicion of something hidden, if he discovers the function of one number, will easily calculate the whole alphabet.

Second, let anyone who desires to be a shrewd practitioner of this matter remember that whenever a letter is doubled in any word, as often happens, it should be written only once and marked above with a point. For example, I wish to write Ioannes from the alphabet of Aries: I do not double 18, which is n, but I write thus: 14. 19. 6. 13. 10. 23.; or abbas: 6 [unclear]. 6. 23.; Ioanes, abas, so that every mark of suspension may be removed. In similar cases, similar caution must be employed; for unless the practitioner is endowed with diligence and knows how to find greater things from small ones, he will not be fit to have these least things of ours disclosed to him.

Not all things are to be communicated indiscriminately to everyone, especially those whose use can be turned to good and evil. Moved reasonably by that consideration, we have plainly handed down many things in these six books of the Polygraphy to those wishing to know, but we have allowed far more secrets to lie hidden beneath manifest things. Finally, we have written out a key that unfolds the whole work, explaining how each metaphor is to be understood; nevertheless, by the advice of certain persons, we have ordered it to remain hidden at home, so that students may not lack material for exercising their memory, and the wicked may be deprived of the means of knowing those things which they are not willing to use well. There lie hidden in each step ...more mysteries; and the greater things you find from these, the greater things remain to be found. A way is prepared for beginners, in which, as they advance, it will not be difficult in the course of time to find many things, both rare and very great. Here one who did not know how will learn to write in Latin, and prudently to wrap all the mysteries of his will in a foreign speech. But that an unlearned man may be able to understand not only his own mysteries which he wraps up, but also open speech, of which until now he has always been ignorant, is a matter of no great labor, if the paraphrast has fully attained our intention in this volume. For beneath the bark lie hidden the kernels of our Steganographia, buried for good reason, lest they lie open to unworthy babblers. Finally, it had been worth the effort that one work should not prejudice the other, but that its own right should be distributed inviolate to each. Wearied after a long voyage, we here cast anchor in the deep under the name of JESUS CHRIST, savior of the faithful, on the twenty-first day of the month of March, in the year of the Lord’s nativity 1508, in the eleventh Roman indiction, at Paeapolis, the city of the East Franks, which they also call Würzburg and Herbipolis.

Here is the end of the sixth book of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot at St. James in Würzburg, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of the divine father Benedict.

Printed at the cost and expense of the most upright bookseller Johannes Haselberg of Aia, of the diocese of Constance, in the year 1518, in the month of July.

Key to the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of St. James of Herbipolis, formerly of Sponheim, of the order of Saint Benedict, of the observance of the fathers of Bursfelde.

With a privilege that it is not to be printed or sold by another for ten years, under penalty as stated in the letters.

Johannes Trithemius.

Preface to the Explanation of the Whole Work of the Polygraphia of Johannes Trithemius, abbot of Paeopolis, that is, Würzburg, at St. James.

No one who has read these things, as I trust, will judge me either proud or superfluous, because I myself have commented on the Polygraphia recently composed by me, especially if he has been able to weigh precisely what cause induced us to speak obscurely. For whatever can do harm when made public had reasonably to be hidden in mystical speech. But the subject which we treat in the Polygraphia is, for the advantage of the commonwealth among good men, very good, useful, and honorable; and for this reason, persuaded by a reasonable cause, we wrote it, so that by its service we might render good men safe and secure from the investigation of the wicked in communicating their secrets to one another. But lest an occasion of deceiving the simpler and less cautious in their judgment of things be offered to wicked and perverse men, who very often abuse even the inventions of the good, we handed down in it mystical or hidden modes of writing, and covered the truth hidden in the marrow with certain coverings of figures. Yet we do not in the least doubt that any industrious man, desirous of these things, will easily grasp everything, if he applies even moderate perseverance in searching them out. For the things I have handed down are neither so difficult nor wrapped in such great mysteries that they cannot be thoroughly penetrated by a studious man. For everywhere we have so tempered the enigmas of our words that they may easily be passable to learned and studious men, while nevertheless remaining inaccessible to lazy men of darkness. But after it pleased us to offer the work of the Polygraphia itself, dedicated, to the most serene and unconquered Caesar of the Romans, Maximilian, ever august emperor of the world, I judged that it would be worthwhile if I made it clear with brief and few interpretations.

and plain, lest the mind of the sacred Majesty, which is daily stretched by many affairs and cares, be drawn away from the understanding of it by the obscurity of mysteries. For, unless my opinion deceives me, the work will be the more welcome and useful to his Majesty the briefer and clearer it is. First, therefore, by the Lord’s bounty, we shall briefly explain the meaning of our purpose, which is contained in the prologue wrapped in various riddles; then, through the individual books of the Polygraphy, we shall set forth succinctly, to the powers of our talent, the modes of working, the rules, cautions, and individual differences, in order, as far as remains necessary.

All these things, so that they may the more quickly become accessible to those who desire to know them, we shall show in sequence by examples, and we shall be as brief as the subject and reason permit.

Key to the Explanation of the Polygraphy of Johannes Trithemius, Abbot of [Peapolis?].

Exposition on the Prologue.

Our whole intention in the entire work of the Polygraphy turns upon this purpose: that we should hand down certain methods of writing secretly, by which kings and princes, nobles and commoners, priests and laymen, learned and unlearned alike, may secretly, safely, and without any suspicion of a hidden secret, by the service of letters, announce to one another and to any friends, even those at a great distance from one another, whatever conception of their minds may be needed, and as often as needed. And lest we seem to have attempted this either first or alone, we forewarn the reader that many of the ancients long ago, especially tyrants, princes, and kings, moved by similar consideration, devised for themselves familiar and various methods and rules of writing, by which they themselves attempted in particular what we have promised universally in our Polygraphy. From their number, for the sake of an example of the proposed matter, we first introduced Caesar Augustus, whose hidden mode of writing take as plainly thus.

He changed the breathings of the conceived voice from clear signs into obscure ones; by a certain fine invention of metathesis, by [unclear], he makes their barbarousness, though resisting the vows, conform to his command. That is: the great Caesar Augustus, so that he might write secretly and safely what he wished, changed the letters of the alphabet by varied transposition, so that he put b for a, c for b, and so consequently with each one. And so that the writing, being more twisted, might remain more secret, he transposed the letters at his pleasure sideways and lengthwise to whatever distance of order, number, and place.

Mystery. And that deceptive order, as though perpetual, subject to the will and to the reckoning of time, although it keeps messengers safe on the road from the assault of [unclear], nevertheless, since it has no regulated limits, makes all who meet them anxious with suspicion of a hidden matter.

Explanation. Although no one can easily comprehend with the understanding the hidden mystery lying beneath the transposition of the letters, nevertheless this writing makes those into whose hands it comes suspicious about the hiding-place of the matter enclosed within.

Mystery. That Archimedes of Syracuse, easily the foremost of mathematicians, made a white bird, suitable to his instructions, naked by head and feet, and the rest.

Explanation. Archimedes had two little rods of one length and thickness planed, round or square, of which he kept one for himself and entrusted the other to his absent friend. And whenever either wished to write something rather secret to the other, he wrapped a white bird, that is, a sheet of papyrus, of small width but of the length of the doubled rod, around the wood, and tied it below and above with wax. Afterwards he wrote on the sheet, continuously from the sides joined artfully together into a mass, whatever he wished; then he loosened the sheet from the rod, and immediately there appeared such a distance between the letters that not even one word cohered with another. He turned the sheet, and when he wished he wrote to himself on the other side. Nor was there anyone ignorant of this device who could have investigated [unclear]. But the man who had the other rod, when he had received the sheet, fastened it on and recalled the letters into their former order.

Mystery. Marcus Tullius Cicero, eloquent orator of the Romans, using talent and art, changed the little elements of phrase into signs, and the rest.

Explanation. He wrote a book of signs for his son, which the blessed martyr Cyprian afterwards enlarged for the use of Christians, namely in the manner of a dictionary …where, according to order, are placed first the characters or notes, and after them the words designated by the same characters, so that any word is signified by a note prefixed to it. With these notes or characters we once saw an entire Latin psalter, beautifully written, in the library of the greater church of Strasbourg; to which some judge of matters, ignorant, had prefixed on the outside a title such as this: "A Psalter in the Armenian tongue." But he erred, since it ought rather to have been written thus: "A Latin Psalter written in Tullian [Tironian] characters." For each character represents one entire Latin word. Nor does the estimation deceive me, since I have by me, written whole in an old volume, the very dictionary of Cicero, emended by Saint Cyprian—incorrupt—which I have nowhere seen elsewhere. And so great is the abundance of notes or characters, with the words subjoined to them, that they altogether suffice for writing in the Latin tongue whatever you wish.

Mystery. Pharamund, the forty-third [king] from Marcomer, king of the Franks, when in the year of the Lord's nativity 424 he powerfully entered the borders of the Gauls, etc. Explanation. The kings of the Franks, from the time when they went out from the Scythian borders, in the year 430 before Christ's nativity, with their people to the mouths of the Rhine—where now Guelderland sits—waged continual war with the Gauls for nearly nine hundred years, and at last violently made them subject [to themselves], as we wrote in the first volume of our annals. Of these [kings], the aforesaid king Pharamund, that he might safely send messengers through the kingdom, devised new letters proper to himself, which no one could understand without his voluntary instruction. And he used not one alphabet only, nor few, but many new alphabets. Mystery. Clodius the Long-haired, son of Pharamund, and after him king of the Franks, who subjugated all Gaul to himself, the Romans being destroyed whom he found in it, used [the cipher-arts] of his father's invention in secret writings. Explanation. This king devised proper and new alphabets, and gave single [ones] to each of his dukes, and retained the knowledge with himself alone. Mystery. Charles by name the Great, the sixty-third king of the Franks, who first of the Franks bore the diadem of the Roman empire, etc. Explanation. He is read to have been born the elder son of king Pippin, duke of Brabant, in the county of Namur, bordering on the Liège-men—although some report him born in the village of Ingelheim, not far from Mainz—[and] he too invented various modes of writing, and, Nanno the grammarian ministering [his] support, devised diverse alphabets, by which he communicated secrets, each in a singular manner, to the several prefects of the kingdom. Mystery. The Normans, once gone out from the borders of Gothia, when they devastated Gaul with cruel invasion, having called owls from Greece, prepared a safe hiding-place for their secrets, etc. Explanation. The Normans, ranging through Gaul (Bede the monk in England testifying), that they might safely write their secrets among themselves, substituted Greek numeral [letters] for the Latin letters, from a, the first, up to the four-and-twentieth, [with] a point such as w or gu, according to the custom of the Gauls. But this mode of writing is altogether most beautiful, in which all the letters are Greek, and according to the Pelasgian order of numbering designate our Latin [letters]: as a = 1, b = 2, c = 3, d = 4, e = 5, f = 6, g = 7, and so consequently up to w, which is 24. This writing neither a Greek will understand, nor a Latin, unless he has first learned the manner of the industrious art. Mystery. Our Bede, a monk in England, not ignorant of what the Normans did, described many [things] like these of the ancients' inventions, by which they made an obscure way lucid through mysteries. He himself [described] arthrology [finger-counting], etc. Explanation. This Bede the monk, in his little book on the inventions of the ancients, recounted many various modes of secretly writing and noting, by which they safely announced their secrets to friends, and spoke without voice to those present. He first of all committed arthrology [and] dactylology [finger-speech] to letters, by the use of which the one most securely discloses to the other whatever secret he wishes—which no one else standing by will note, and much less understand. That this very [thing] can be done in many other ways, Bede himself taught; concerning which, since we have written nothing in the Polygraphy, we here deservedly refuse to say more. A proper place for these very arduous matters we long ago assigned in the Steganography, which we do not yet think to publish. And who could express all the modes of the ancients' secret writing? For some had as familiars, in the ministry of the aforesaid art, "owls" [bubones] called Philophoti [light-lovers], others Mysophoti [light-haters], others called both into practice by [the] art; again others transposed the known letters of the common alphabet; others, under the guise of barbarians, devised proper characters for themselves.

others used the service of visible letters, writing with minium or with common ink, while others formed invisible characters at their own will, at a nod. The methods of visible characters for secret writing are exceedingly many, and altogether innumerable; to make mention of them all is neither our wish nor within our power. Of invisible characters, however, there are three kinds more commonly used among mortals today. The first is called Dermatic, by which a certain artificial writing is made on the backs of messengers, visible only by the washing of a certain fluid; no one can penetrate it who does not know the secret of the art. The second is called Hyphasmatic, by which one writes on cloth with certain substances; when dried, it cannot be seen at all until, moistened in cold water, it is perceived. The third kind is named Alleotic; it is manifold and varied, both in form and in material, and has almost innumerable methods of writing secretly. Its writing is made on paper or without paper, with [unclear], with [unclear], and with various other things. Letters likewise are written in various ways and hidden in places, as under [unclear], under [unclear], in [unclear], in [unclear], in [unclear], [unclear], in [unclear], in [unclear], and in other almost infinite things of the same sort. But because none of these things at this time serves our purpose, we must therefore hasten to those things which reason requires. There is another kind, Dactiletron, not of writing, however, but of signs, by which, in very subtle ways, one can communicate to another the conception of his mind. This itself is varied by so many differences that there is no one in the world who could enumerate all the species of so great a mystery. By the principal method, together with many others descending from it, one may, by art, while sitting at table or in any other place, securely and most safely communicate whatever one wishes to a person who knows the art, without anyone’s suspicion. Finally, how without letters you may disclose the secret of your mind to one absent, even when the very person who performs the office of messenger does not know it, remains written among the inventions of steganography. For indeed, since kings and princes encounter many affairs, knowledge of which they sometimes do not trust to give safely enough by customary letters to their deputies far away, it will be worthwhile for each of them to have some special methods of writing and announcing, by which they may most safely make their secrets known to friends, especially in these times, in which, with license to sin prevailing, nowhere in the world is secure faith found.

Messengers of princes are seized everywhere by savage robbers; they are plundered, beaten, and for the most part killed. Nor do the impious robbers spare even the letters of kings, closed and sealed with rings. Therefore it would be necessary for your commonwealth, O most glorious Emperor Maximilian, that you put on the skin of Hercules and brandish the club in your hands, and purge the world committed to you by God of these savage monsters. There will never be peace in the kingdom unless the [unclear] are removed from the midst. He who disturbs the peace of the kingdom shows himself to be the king’s enemy. These are the robbers who beset the roads of travelers and seize others’ property; the earth is full of them today, and nowhere is the road safe for those who walk.

Brief Explanation of Those Things Which Seem More Obscure in the First Book of the Polygraphia

Although nothing obscure is contained in the first book of the Polygraphia, nevertheless, lest its composition perhaps seem profound to simpler readers, we briefly explain those things which are thought more difficult. We have distributed the words of the Latin language, in order, more than nine thousand of them, under almost four hundred alphabets, in such a sequence that if from each alphabet only one word after another is taken from the beginning to the end, cohering mutually with one another they will produce a fitting Latin discourse. For it will be a very suitable method of writing most secretly whatever we wish, since each word represents the letter placed before it at the head. Nor should it trouble you, reader, that a multitude of words in the open contains a brief meaning in secret, since in this childish arrangement of ours there lies hidden a higher method of writing whatever you wish, much more broadly and much more secretly, which public reason has forbidden us to make plain to all. But whoever is endowed with talent and applies the necessary powers to inquiry will find, hidden in these teachings, subtler things wonderfully unknown before; he will plainly understand wonders. Nevertheless this suitable method of writing will suffice for all things, since the narration, though repeated so many times, is varied. For, as we said, from the first alphabet you take one word, and from the second likewise one, thus successively one from each, and one from those interposed outside the ordered line, up to the period or the end of the book, and a Latin discourse sufficiently fitting will arise for you. But care must be taken that at one time and all at once no more than one word be taken from one alphabet, and that the writer, through negligence or excessive haste, not skip over some alphabet and confuse the order of the narrative. By day understand the open narrative, but by night the hidden, secret one, which should not be very long but brief. The examples that follow in the text, concerning the invisible soul and the body that is seen, pertain to both narratives, the hidden and the manifest. As often as “the leaf is moved by the wind,” and the rest, we advise that you count the secret narrative with reference to the open one, so that both may end together at the close of each period. But if anything should remain over from the secret matter, let it be enlarged with such moderation that both narratives end at one point, lest a confusion of eclipse be produced. The remaining points that follow in the first lesson of the explanation of the Polygraphy are all implicitly referred to the things we have said. It must also be noted that under the order of the alphabets no word is vacant, but each represents the letter set before it at the head. So that the reader may not lack full knowledge of this matter, let us explain the sense by an example. Let us suppose the case that a worthless man asks, through you, to be advanced with some friend of yours; but you, in order to cut off importunate requests and yet not promote an unworthy man, determine to write more secretly to your friend through the petitioner himself, so that he may not understand: “Beware of that fellow, because he is a thief, a most wicked scoundrel.” Go to the first alphabet and write the word Conditor, which signifies C; in the second, clemens, which [unclear]; in the third, discernens, which represents [unclear]; in the fourth, mundana, signifies e. Now you have, in the hidden narrative, “beware.” Proceed consequently also through the other alphabets, [unclear] such a discourse: “The gracious Creator, discerning worldly things, may he impart seraphic pleasantness to those who ask, with all his saints in heaven, amen. The gentleness of the most glorious prince, everywhere reverently to be remembered by the saints, [unclear] by the best precepts us, most abject, [unclear] of the director of good things, to abandon, to await with every affection the glory of perpetual rest [unclear]. Therefore, O vain mockers, receive with instruction, [so that?] you may be able to enter the most blessed rejoicings of the archangels of the orthodox rewarder, most blessed in comeliness. Therefore flee back from the foulest honors of this pilgrimage, since you are most holily about to enter the most blessed delights of the kindly savior of the ages.” In this foregoing public narrative there is contained this sentence lying hidden in secret, namely: “Beware of that man, because he is a thief and a wicked, most vile fellow; but be silent, I pray.” Proceed in the same order as long as it is in all other cases whatsoever, and one must begin from the head as often as necessary, until you have enclosed the hidden narrative of your mystery openly. But the words that are placed outside the alphabetical order designate no letter, nor do they serve the hidden narrative, but they have been interposed because of a lack of synonyms, so that the sequence of the Latin discourse might be completed. For we were not always able to have so many words with the same signification, especially among pronouns, conjunctions, prepositions, and interjections, that in place of the twenty-four wandering letters we could have made an alphabet, as is clearly evident after the eighth alphabet, where we placed two words outside the order, lest we leave the discourse defective. For thus we placed: “With all.” Thus: “When you live.” Of these the writer may take the two he wishes, so that the Latin discourse may be completed. Let him do likewise in the other cases, whenever he finds similar ones. We have adopted double w on account of our native speech, since we frequently need it in our German language. For he who is ignorant of the Latin language may write his hidden secret in German under a Latin discourse without any difficulty.

Now follow the rules or cautions to be observed in the operation of this book.

The first rule or caution warns you that the secret of your mind which you wish to announce to an absent friend, one who knows the art and has the book of Polygraphy, you should write as diligently as you can on a slip of paper, in the Latin language or in German, or in any other language you wish, provided it can be comprised in Roman letters. Then With the sheet written in this way, place it before you, so that for the individual letters of the secret you may suitably fit a word. For, as we have shown, in this practice of writing a whole word is taken. We gave an example a little earlier in the foregoing.

II. The second caution directs you that, as has been said, you should not take more than one word at a time from any alphabet in one narrative of public Latin speech; otherwise you would both confuse the open meaning and wholly draw away from understanding of the mystery the friend to whom you had written.

III. Thirdly, take the greatest care that through negligence you do not pass over any alphabet from which you do not take one word appropriate to the secret. Likewise provision must be made that whenever one word or more occurs outside the sequence of the alphabet, you take the whole upper line, or the lower, and not both.

IV. Fourthly, care must be taken that whenever the discourse of the open speech has been brought to a complete sentence, the following sentence should take its beginning from a larger, thickened letter, according to the form of the preceding example, in which, according to the sense of the Latin discourse, we took capital letters at the beginning and small letters in the rest, in the common manner. When the secret of your mind is long, so that it exceeds the narrative of the open speech, if much remains you should begin again from the beginning; if little remains, the discourse may be brought back at pleasure from any place whatever. For no one even moderately skilled in this craft will be able not to know where you have begun again. Nor is there need to fear the harmony of the speech, since it will always be varied by the manifest narrative together with the hidden one; whenever a beginning is made from the start, a new face of the discourse will follow. A continuation can also be made from the end of the first book through the second.

V. Fifthly, we advise that whenever you wish to write in earnest by this art, you prepare for yourself a small book in which you write your secret mystery in manifest discourse. Whoever sees or reads this little book will not think that any secret lies hidden, nor, if he has a suspicion, will he be able to find anything of what you write.

VI. Sixthly, it should be noted that if, throughout the whole Polygraphia, you transpose the order of the words in each alphabet by changing the arrangement, and if you write two volumes according to it, one for yourself and the other for any friend, you will write between yourselves, with complete security, whatever you wish, nor is there any man living on earth who could penetrate your secrets. This transposition, however, can be made in infinite ways.

VII. Seventhly, we forewarn you that one must write polygraphically in one way to a man ignorant of the Latin language, and in another way to one skilled in it. For the former all words must be written out in full, without abbreviation, distinctly, completely, beautifully, and altogether legibly, without separation, without division, without confusion, lest, deceived by error, he think one word to be two, or suppose two to be one. The things that are set down must be heeded.

VIII. Eighthly, provision must be made that the person to whom you write mystically by this art should have a book wholly like yours; otherwise you would write in vain and fruitlessly to one who does not understand.

IX. Ninthly, if you wish this craft to remain forever secret and hidden, write out the Polygraphia anew, but do not place the letters of the alphabet before the words; no one will easily suspect the method of the secret. But so that no difficulty in the mystery may occur to the writer or reader, let the letters of the alphabet be written on a small sheet in the order corresponding to the words, and let it be fitted movably to the headings of the same words. The letters can also be engraved on a copper plate, so that they may be moved from one order to another.

X. Tenthly, it should be known that although we do not use the Pythagorean y in German and Latin words, nevertheless we have admitted it on account of the Greek language, so that we might have the twelvefold number doubled. Likewise we have received the doubled w as the twenty-fourth letter, which for us is altogether necessary in the German language.

XI. Eleventhly, let the person who receives letters written from the Polygraphia to be read know that intelligence is needed in the reading. And therefore, whenever he takes up a sheet or little book written polygraphically, let him go to a secret place, and, opening the book of the Polygraphia which he must have with him, let him consider each word through all the alphabets, and what letter each one represents; with chalk upon a table, or with ink on paper, let him note it very carefully. And when he has examined the whole letter in that way, let him put the letters together into words, and he will easily understand what lay hidden in secret.

XII. Twelfthly, let kings and princes note, who have many vicars in different places, to all of whom it is not safe to write with one kind of hidden narrative. Therefore, so that they may have their own secret mode of writing to each one individually, let them change the order of the words as many times as

[unclear] to have separate ones. And thus they themselves will possess all the methods of writing, and none of the subjects will understand another’s method. For the variable methods of writing more secretly in this art are infinite.

Thirteenth, it should be noted that, to stop the mouths of those who speak unjustly, we show the truth of this new invention of ours to be possible by placing the words in the alphabets of the first book so that they cohere with one another, and in the manner of an exhortation and supplication offered to God they produce a fitting and Latin prayer. Under its narrative we can conceal whatever secrets occur to us, and write in such a way to a friend skilled in the art that, if all the men in the whole world were to come together into one place, they would never be able to find the secret lying hidden beneath the open discourse, provided it has been arranged correctly.

Fourteenth, it should be known that in this very invention of our Polygraphy there still lie hidden certain things far better than those written above, namely how you will be able, in a few days, not to say hours, to instruct one ignorant of the Latin language so that he knows how to write, read, speak, and understand Latin, not indeed all things universally, but in a certain manner whatever necessary thing may occur to him on any subject in his affairs. Likewise, how you may make known to your friend far absent, and knowing the practice of the art, all the conceptions of your mind safely, securely, and most secretly, without writings and without the messenger’s knowledge, sometimes even naturally without a messenger and without any superstition, danger, or fear. But reason has moved us that these things remain buried, hidden with the rest in their own concealment, since it neither pleases me nor is at all expedient to cast precious stones, once found, away, and to accomplish difficult things without the fruit of gratitude. Finally, there lie hidden beneath these no small mysteries of subtlety concerning medicines, herbs, plants, precious stones, rivers, the members of the human body, brute animals, saints, nations, cosmography, astronomy and the seven liberal arts, also concerning all these things that are held in human use, and concerning the universal world, both of visible and invisible things. And lest we be more lengthy than is right: all things that are in the world, through the enlargement of demonstrated likeness, serve the mystical teaching of the art of Polygraphy.

Fifteenth, note that all these things which we have transmitted as discovered in the Polygraphy are certain small introductions in comparison with those which still remain to be discovered and written in this same faculty; concerning these we pass over in silence, lest we seem to boast vainly. For we have given to those endowed with talent an occasion for discovering greater things than we have either written or perhaps have been able to discover. Let him who can add, for the completion of this invention, the things which he knows to be useful; but let him who cannot do so not rashly judge things he does not understand.

An explanation of those things which seemed rather obscure in the second book of the Polygraphy.

In the second book of the Polygraphy, apart from the order and sequence of the words, nothing new is handed down from the first, and for that reason there will be one and the same method of working in both. All the things which we said in the first book had to be observed, we carefully advise must also be observed in the second. Only in the narrative of the prayer is a manifest difference seen to have arisen, since the former is composed concerning our Lord, the Son of God, whereas this one is raised to his mother, the ever-untouched Virgin. In the second book, moreover, three hundred and eight alphabets are set in order before the words, under different subjects. For from the beginning the narrative of the discourse is directed to that Lady of ours; afterwards the Lord’s Prayer is expanded under twenty-four alphabets; then the angelic salutation is appended; consequently the Salve Regina; and last a brief prayer concerning Saint Anne, mother of the Virgin Mary, parent of God. In all books of the Polygraphy one must beware lest a single word be duplicated in any alphabetical order, that is, lest it be placed twice, or lest any be omitted, because it would make great confusion for the reader. Therefore one must take the greatest care that the copies be in every respect emended and corrected exactly, lest you fall into error while writing. But if, through the negligence of the scribe or the carelessness of the printer, you find some word duplicated under one alphabet, erase the last one and put in its place another suitable word which has not already been in the same alphabet. Know also that these two books of our Polygraphy sufficiently serve the promised operation; through them you may not only write most safely and securely to friends whatever you wish at any time you will be able to announce, but also, without any suspicion, to make a man wholly ignorant of the Latin language, provided only that he knows how to form letters, an instructed participant in this art, something which we believe had previously been unheard of in such a manner. But because this method of writing secretly, under a long narrative of open discourse, comprises rather few statements of hidden intention, it will perhaps be usable only in great and difficult matters, especially among those to whom leisure is pleasing and labor displeasing. We shall therefore give, in the four following books, easier methods of writing, although they are by no means free from the suspicion of observers, because they are far removed from understanding and [unclear].

In the Steganographia, however, the methods of writing very secretly without any suspicion are more abundant, where a word does not represent a letter, but each word represents another whole word suitable to the mystery. Let us set down an example of this: if you wish to forewarn a friend about some imminent danger, under such a narrative of words: Melancius, Tyberius, Ioannes Petrus, servants of the count de Asoto, have conspired to kill you; on the fourth day after Lawrence, at night, they will surround your house; consider what you should do. Steganography conceals this secret as follows: I beg you, dearest friend, to send me by the bearer of the present letter ten florins as a loan, because they are very necessary to me for the construction of a certain building; I shall faithfully repay them to you. Who would seek or suspect that this secret lay hidden in the discourse written above? Let us set down the same thing also in another narrative. Lord Jesus Christ, Son of the living God, who for our sake wished to become man, to suffer, and to die, have mercy on me, an unworthy sinner, now in the perishable hour of my death. Behold, now you have one hidden thought of your heart, veiled under the bounds of steganography in a faithful brevity of speech, in a twofold narrative; the whole world will not even be able to suspect it, nor, if it sought for a hundred years, to find it in any way, even if all the learned came together. Finally, steganography teaches you to hide this very secret thought of your heart not only in one or two of the narratives written above, but in almost infinitely many, by the method now described, and to announce it to whomever you wish most safely, most secretly, and most securely. All methods of this kind of invention can also be changed by metathesis in infinite variations, and by them everything can be written and announced. But why the work on steganography remains buried in silence has been sufficiently said at the beginning of our Polygraphia; therefore it was not to be repeated here. Let it lie hidden, then, lest it be seen by the ungrateful.

An explanation of the obscure matters contained in the third book of our Polygraphia.

In the third book of the Polygraphia we have handed down a newly devised method of secret writing, sufficiently safe and secure indeed, but suspect to all observers of containing a hidden secret. For no one, however learned, will discover the hidden mystery without knowledge of the instruction, since he cannot even understand the open writing. We arrange fabricated words, representing nothing in themselves, but only the letters of the alphabet set before them; by means of these you will be able to write and make known all the secrets of your mind to a friend, however far absent, with the greatest safety. But the unskilled and ignorant of the art, when they see the writing, will think it is some foreign language, and will be utterly ignorant of what it contains. When you wish to write or announce something to an absent person according to the method of this book, take care first of all that you properly separate every single word from the others, so that each one can be most clearly distinguished from another, lest the person to whom you write take one word for two, or two for one, because that would produce a great error. Let us set down an example of this: Abrin madon badis, cadulur pasu, adin loroff masara damis, boda omo dromi drus mastron pha lares medas raffut ma debor tara, mesen baiu phofat, galos, prosol fane lemoros, aroso habilneso, hamol heliet rhamil fesia doron hubur rodex. In this narrative of fictitious speech there is contained this brief hidden statement of a friend warning a friend of danger: Do not come to court, because the king is angry with you. You see that this method of writing and announcing whatever you wish to a friend who understands it is easy, safe, and secure. In all cases, however, you should know that care must be taken, as was said before, lest again you skip over any alphabet. As often as the narrative B iij

[unclear] of the fabricated discourse to the end of the book, the secret of your mind not yet completed, you should begin again from the beginning, and do this as often as will be necessary. Nevertheless, each person will be able, at his own discretion, to change, alter, improve these words of ours, and add more, yet in such a way that he avoids a sequence of sound breaking out disgracefully into words.

Explanation of the fourth book of our Polygraphia.

In the fourth book of the Polygraphia, in similar fashion, we have placed words fabricated by us in alphabetical order, but in one thing alone we deliberately differ from the preceding book. For in the preceding book the words contain no property in themselves other than that they represent the letters set before them at the head. But in the fourth book, which we now have in hand, each word contains its own force, and nevertheless designates the letters placed before it. Within it has what they show without, because the second letter of each word always serves the hidden mystery, which we shall make plain by the following example. Ecorach banasar dulay semalas, chorion suriel anephor schabarbas, busarat uimalo tropon tumelech amasar. For understanding the mystery of this, take only the second letter from each word, and you will find this hidden meaning: Beware this man. For the second letter in Ecorach is c, in banasar a, in dulay u, in semalas e. Join these four letters and they will make this word: Caue. And so one should proceed in the rest up to the end of the book; and if any hidden mystery remains to be written, one should return to the beginning as often as necessary, until the secret has been completed in full. In this very secret manner of writing, if someone has been practiced by long use, he does not need the book, but will easily compose on the spot words suited to his purpose. But one who is less practiced in composition necessarily requires a copy of the book from which he may write. The reader will not need a copy of the volume, since without the book, by means of the second letters everywhere, he can easily find the hidden secret. Yet in great, difficult, or dangerous matters, this manner of writing will not be trusted with sufficient safety, because by the diligence of a skilled man the hidden mystery could be discovered by chance. This manner of writing can also be changed by an intelligent man, so that the signifying letters are placed in the third or fourth position of the word, with the words altered.

Brief explanation for the fifth book of our Polygraphia.

[unclear]

In the fifth book of the Polygraphia we have handed down various modes of writing secretly through the transposition of common letters, arranged in such a coordination that under their covering we shall be able safely to write and report everything to an absent friend. Now, to speak in our customary manner, the progression of the transposition of letters is almost infinite, since innumerable things arise from one alphabet by metathesis. First we have described a straight table containing twenty-four alphabets; through understanding it, as many alphabets will be able to be composed as there are stars numbered in the firmament of heaven. For as many letters as there are in that table, so many times, by the art, hundreds of thousands of alphabets arise in order. After this we distribute a reversed table, which will arise into another as often as you change the first letter at the head. The first letter in the straight table is b, in the reversed one z. As often as you put any other varied letter in their place, so often you will find a table new in every respect, and so on to infinity. Then we expand the first straight table, placing at the head of each transposed black letter, in red, the letter that it represents, so that we might provide the reader with an easier method of writing. This is the method of writing: from the first black alphabet take one letter of the hidden sentence, from the second another, from the third a third, and so in succession up to the end. When you have reached it, remember to return as often as necessary to the first order, until by concealment you have completed the secret mystery of your mind. But so that you may see the order, let us set down an example. Hxpf gfbmcʒ fucib gmbt gxhsr ege rbd qopma uwu. wfxegk ak.tnr qxyx. Of this mystical discourse the mean

[unclear] is: Beware this man, because he is evil, a thief, a deceiver, a liar, and wicked. You now see, reader, what a remarkable transposition of the letters of the alphabet this table produces, since there is no one who, without knowledge of it, could penetrate this secret. For this manner of writing surpasses every common transposition of letters, since each letter is always changed from one series of the alphabet into another. From the reversed table also, which we have set out in order with a similar distribution, let us place such an example by way of introduction: Rdkt, st[unclear]nyb, tevqj, sn[unclear]f, fdrgh, vfd. Its hidden meaning is this: Beware this man, because he is evil. And note that, under the example of the direct table already given, we have drawn the hidden series from the beginning through the whole of it, and then, by continuing in like manner through the reversed table, we again make a circle, as you see, to the beginning of the direct table. Hence it must be considered that one series of writing can be drawn through both tables, just as we have already done in the demonstration of the first example; or, if you prefer, through one only, as we have shown sufficiently in the reversed table. Nor will it cause difficulty for the reader to whom you send your hidden message, for he will easily understand everything if he has had even a little experience in the art. But the strongest instruction, which increases knowledge, is practice frequently repeated in any art.

After the setting out of the tables, certain orchemata follow, in which there is not only a transposition of all the letters, but also an ordered leaping of one over another. For orchema in Greek is called transilitio, “leaping across,” in Latin. And first, indeed, we marked the leap of the letters in the expanded form; afterward we reduced it into an orchema. In the operation of this orchema there is a remarkable leap. In it there are twenty-four alphabets. In the first no letter intervenes. In the second, one. In the third, two. In the fourth, three. In the fifth, four. In the sixth, five. In the seventh, six. In the eighth, seven. In the ninth, nine. Finally in the eleventh, ten, and so consequently up to the twenty-fourth alphabet, in which twenty-three letters intervene; afterward a return of likeness is made to the beginning. But the manner of writing by orchemata for the mystery is similar to that observed in the tables of transposition of letters: namely, that one who is about to write according to the rule of the orchema should take from each alphabet only one black letter, which the writing in red shows from the head. For understanding this, let us give an example: Prdh. ifyqyn. bdyen. zhkt. sxsol. inq. Its meaning is this: Beware this man, because he is evil.

When in writing you have come to the end of the orchemata, and the begun secret of your heart has not yet been completed, you must know that you are to return to the beginning as often as needed, until the mystery has been completed through everything. And know that from one orchema of letters as many alphabets are composed as an inquirer may have wished, however studiously, to have. Finally, this method of writing by orchemata, that is, by leapings-across and leaps, is the safest of all, because the transposition of the letters arises not uniform but varied in many ways. And it should be noted that a true and perfect knowledge of the little tables and the orchemata, if you are industrious and studious, will give you understanding of all writings that are written in any manner by transposition of letters. And it is a great secret, which few have known, that all meanings hidden in any transposition of letters whatever can be discovered.

Brief Explanation of the Sixth and Last Book of the Polygraphy.

In the sixth and last book of the Polygraphy we have assembled certain characters of the ancients, which they used in place of letters, so that, if anyone wishes to take from it an alphabet of his own for himself, he may be able to do so, although one moderately skilled may, if he wishes, devise for himself much more beautiful characters. All the synthemata of this book are sufficiently open and clear, and therefore need no explanation, or only a brief one. Yet those which stand forth as newly invented by us require a definite declaration, lest perhaps they seem to have been set down without reason. First of all, we made all the letters of the Latins numerical, after the custom of the Hebrews and the Greeks, thinking it shameful for us if we should be found inferior to them in this respect. For what is it that we have doubled certain letters so that they might suffice for an infinite number, when the Jews, compelled long ago by the same necessity, did this very thing? And the Greeks, because of a lack of letters, admitted certain signs into number, since they could not double letters. But we, because we are pressed by an equal lack of letters, [unclear] for et; nor does it matter whether it is written thus, et, or thus, &, provided it represents six in number. But we have added another, 9, which our people, when abbreviating, [unclear].

they write it for con and com indifferently; here, in the order of numbers, it represents six hundred. Moreover, by the same necessity we have doubled two letters, namely r, z, s, s; of these, r signifies ninety, while curved z signifies one hundred, long s two hundred, and closed s three hundred. Further, w, born as a double letter, which for this reason, by the usage of the German tongue, we have placed in the order of the alphabet, represents the last letter, in the series of numbers, one thousand.

Let us set down a tabular example of this new invention of ours for the reckoning of numbers, so that anyone who wishes to know the method may have a definite proof before his eyes. For what has always been easy for the Hebrews and Greeks will not be impossible for us. The table of numbers follows.
